headlines.summary: Lowe's said it saw strength in online sales during its quarter that contributed to a guidance raise for the full year.
headlines.article_text: Lowe's (LOW) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Lowe's said it saw strength in online sales during its quarter that contributed to a guidance raise for the full year. The home improvement retailer said it's also seeing strength among its professional shoppers. The company said it received roughly $250 million in tariff benefits during the quarter. In this article LOW Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:58 06:58 Lowe’s posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market Squawk Box Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers. The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion. Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat. CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years. "We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC. Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers. He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects. "We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program." Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.10 adjusted, it was not immediately clear if that compared to the $2.88 expected Revenue: $22.76 billion vs. $22.41 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior. The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates. Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year. Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter. "So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said. Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far. Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth. Gary Hershorn | Corbis News | Getty Images A series of tech outages has consumers stocking up on emergency supplies. Costco sales are seeing a lift because of it, according to research firm Mizuho. In the final week of October, Mizuho estimates Costco's U.S. comparable sales, excluding gasoline, rose 11% to 12%, up from the normal 6% to 7% the first three weeks in October. Costco reported an 8.1% increase for the month. The firm said the stronger pace is continuing through November as 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators it tracked on Costco's website sold out as of Sunday night. Shares of Costco were roughly flat-to-lower in Wednesday morning trading around $1,107 apiece. "Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at COST," said Mizuho analyst David Bellinger in a research note Monday. Bellinger will appear on CNBC's "The Exchange" during the 1pm hour. The stockpiling intensified from a series of recent disruptions . Microsoft's Outlook and Teams outage on Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nation-wide on Friday. A separate software outage at JPMorgan Chase Monday caused banking transaction delays while a system outage delayed United Airlines flights Monday. The National Security Agency on Tuesday said the spy agency's communication network went down temporarily. The various outages appear to come amid a rush to recover software vulnerabilities uncovered by AI tools and officials are saying there's no reason for panic. Still, on TikTok and other social media platforms, posts urging people to stock up on food and supplies are gaining significant traction. Mizuho raised its price target on Costco to $1,150 from $1,100 and kept its buy-equivalent outperform rating. The firm said U.S. comparable sales could grow more than 10% in November. Mizuho also sees Walmart 's Sam's Club benefiting from emergency preparedness sales as shoppers fill up their pantries, and for Home Depot and Lowe's as they buy home improvement emergency supplies. At Costco, Mizuho will be watching whether the surge brought in new members sign-ups when the warehouse retailer reports its first quarter of fiscal 2027 on Dec. 10. headlines.article_text: Anthropic IPO: AI lab considers increasing offering Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic is considering upsizing its IPO, according to people familiar with the details. The AI lab is expected to set its final IPO price after market close on Wednesday. The stock is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" on Thursday. In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Anthropic Co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei speaks during INBOUND 2025 Powered by HubSpot at Moscone Center on Sept. 4, 2025 in San Francisco, California. Chance Yeh | Getty Images Anthropic is considering upsizing its IPO, people familiar with the details told CNBC, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80. The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The orders are indications of interest and are not binding. All of the details are subject to change, and Anthropic will make final decisions on Wednesday afternoon, the people said. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close on Wednesday. Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX , even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion. The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range. A representative for Anthropic declined to comment. Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, whether as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD. "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time." Amodei co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO. "Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort." Retail investor enthusiasm for Anthropic IPO to rival SpaceX debut
headlines.summary: Anthropic is gearing up for a blockbuster initial public offering this week, and excitement among retail investors looks to be off the charts.
headlines.article_text: Anthropic IPO: Retail investor demand boom Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Vanda Research estimates about $250 million of net retail buying on Anthropic’s first trading day, a forecast twice the size of the SpaceX IPO. Anthropic is expected to begin trading on Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker ANT after plans to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each. The bar for success is lower for Anthropic than SpaceX, as it comes at a time with the AI trade in turmoil. watch now VIDEO 7:59 07:59 Why retail investors are divided over Anthropic's IPO Markets and Politics Digital Original Video Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate. "I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said. Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO. "That would be far and away the largest amount of net retail buying of any stock that we've seen in our data on the first day of its listing," Jai Malhi, senior strategist at Vanda, said in an interview with CNBC. The artificial intelligence laboratory — which will trade on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol ANT — is selling 825 million shares at an expected price range of $70 to $78 per share in the IPO, though sources told CNBC the stock is likely to price above that range . Individual investors are expected to be allocated as much as 20% in that initial offering. And if Vanda's figures prove correct, the buying enthusiasm will be big as regular trading begins. Founded less than six years ago, Anthropic aims to raise as much as $64.4 billion, giving it a valuation of $1.405 trillion. If demand is especially strong, Anthropic could even raise more than the record $85.7 billion that SpaceX sold in its record IPO in June. The tech trade has been in turmoil since Jensen Huang's departure last week as Nvidia CEO raised questions about the future of AI financing. Before then, a potential slowdown in data center development resulting from Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, and signs of moderation in the capital expenditures boom, had already spooked investors. These all stand in marked contrast to the market backdrop in place at the time of the SpaceX IPO. In June, both positioning and sentiment were high, Malhi said. The Anthropic IPO could see a different dynamic, however. Demand could be strong across the entire investor spectrum given that sentiment is depressed, meaning that the bar to beat expectations is "much easier to overcome," he explained. "What we're seeing across both retail and institutional positioning is that there is plenty of dry powder to take part in this IPO," the strategist said. 'Pure-play AI leader' For the 27-year-old New Yorker Shetty, who himself works at agentic data platform Data Workers, this is his first time vying to take part in an IPO. He said Anthropic's emphasis on "safety first" drew his interest. "I've been telling all of my friends, 'If you have like $5, you should invest it in this stock because this is the pure-play AI leader,'" Shetty said. "I think of my father who invested in Microsoft during the dotcom bubble, and he divested from that stock, and it was such a silly thing to do." Not everyone agrees. Joe Pak, a former macro portfolio manager who is now an independent researcher outside London, is opting against participating in the Anthropic IPO for two reasons: the likelihood of limited allocation and current macroeconomic conditions. He believes the odds are probably stacked against retail investors when it comes to the allocation of shares. "It's very difficult as a retail investor to actually get an allocation in these blockbuster IPOs," the 36-year-old said. "You get maybe one share, and the base case is you don't get any at all. So, it's a bit of a catch-22. If you do get a lot of shares, it probably means that the institutional bid was weaker, and in that case, you don't actually want the shares at that level." In terms of the economy, conditions "need to be favorable" to hold a position in a stock like Anthropic, he said. But with the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September and widely expected to do so again next month, the backdrop could be darkening. "From a price-to-sales ratio, Anthropic's like a really good deal. ... [But] it's still a massive valuation for a $1.4 trillion company, and there are significantly better deals out there if you are a fundamental investor." Russ Faigen Retail investor "The risk that you have is the financial conditions deteriorating" before the company starts to grow into anticipated profit and revenue, which would justify purchase of the stock, Pak said. While Pak is steering clear of the IPO, he did say that at a certain level, it would make sense to get into Anthropic. Other retail investors such as Bryan Nearnberg share Pak's view. "I'm planning to eventually buy Anthropic, just not at the IPO price, considering when the lockups expire and there's some selling pressure," said the 37-year-old Westchester County resident, who works in finance operations. "We are not at the end of this short-term negative headline sentiment." IPOs are a sore spot for Nearnberg, who hasn't had much luck trading stocks on their opening day. His skepticism toward IPOs can be traced all the way back to when he was in college. "I didn't get an allocation to the Facebook IPO, but I ended up buying it the first day of open. I got burned pretty quickly," Nearnberg told CNBC. "Same thing with Zynga. I didn't get an allocation, but [got] burned pretty quickly in terms of price." As a result of those experiences, "I'm pretty sure we'll see a good entry price underneath the IPO for Anthropic by Memorial Day next year," Nearnberg said, citing sour sentiment toward technology and concern surrounding circular financing as short-term headwinds. Waiting game To be clear, all the retail investors CNBC spoke with are optimistic on AI as a transformative technology — even the ones sitting out the IPO. One trader said he believes in AI so much that he uses Anthropic's Claude, a conversational AI assistant, every day. But Russ Faigen, a 27-year-old in Austin, Texas, is undecided on whether to subscribe for a piece of the IPO. "From a price-to-sales ratio, Anthropic's like a really good deal," Faigen said. But "it's still a massive valuation for a $1.4 trillion company, and there are significantly better deals out there if you are a fundamental investor." Faigen, who works for an agentic brokerage firm, said he's "leaning towards patience," as he believes Anthropic is going to be public "for a very long time." "I just am not in a rush to get in on day one based off the valuation," he told CNBC. Anthropic's valuation depends on its ability to sustain its rapid growth. In the nine months through Sept. 30, revenue reached more than $33 billion, 1,200% above the year-earlier period. Aggregate spending commitments total about $900 billion , primarily centered around computing power and infrastructure. Breakneck growth leads plenty of retail and institutional investors to approach not just the Anthropic IPO but the entire AI trade with caution. "A lot of it comes down to scrutiny over how much money they're spending on AI," said Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst at eToro. "Investors want to see that those investments are turning into tangible returns, into tangible revenue."
